purpose: A resistor with a moving wiper contact. It creates an adjustable voltage divider, allowing users to dial in continuous analog voltages from 0V to 5V (0 to 1023 in code) or calibrate analog sensor thresholds.

whenToUse.scenario: User Input Control Knobs (Volume, Speed, LED Dimming)
whenToUse.why: When a project needs intuitive human control for motor speed, audio volume, or lamp brightness. Outer pins connect to 5V and GND, wiper connects to A0 for reading 0–1023.
Standard 16x2 HD44780 LCD screens are completely blank or solid black unless the V0 contrast pin is fed ~0.5V to 1V. A pot trimmer dials in the perfect crispness.

whenToUse.scenario: Analog Sensor Sensitivity Trimmer (PIR, Sound, Flame)
whenToUse.why: Used on breakout sensor boards so you can calibrate the exact distance, sound level, or darkness threshold that triggers the digital output.
Human hearing perceives volume exponentially. Using a linear pot makes volume jump suddenly. An audio (logarithmic) taper pot increases volume smoothly to our ears.
whenToUse.recommended: 10 kΩ or 100 kΩ Logarithmic Potentiometer (A10K / A100K)

basics.title: What it is
basics.text: A resistor with a knob. Turning the knob moves a contact, called the wiper, along a resistive track, so you choose how the resistance is shared.

basics.title: Three pins
basics.text: The two outer pins are the ends of the track; the resistance between them never changes (e.g. 10 kΩ). The middle pin is the wiper that moves.

basics.title: As a voltage divider
basics.text: Outer pins to 5V and GND, middle pin to A0. Turning the knob gives any voltage from 0 to 5V, which the Nano reads as 0–1023.

basics.title: As a variable resistor
basics.text: Use one outer pin and the wiper to get an adjustable resistance, e.g. to set an LED's brightness or a sensor's threshold.

basics.title: Which value for Arduino
basics.text: Use 10 kΩ. The Nano's analog input works best when the source is 10 kΩ or less; bigger pots work, but readings can be a little noisier.

basics.title: Never short it
basics.text: When you use only two pins, add a fixed resistor in series. At the end of the turn the resistance becomes 0 Ω, which can short your supply or burn an LED.

howToRead: Look for a letter and a value, e.g. B10K. The letter is the taper (how the value changes as you turn) and the number is the full resistance.
B = linear, A = logarithmic (audio), C = reverse logarithmic.
K means × 1000 and M means × 1 000 000: 10K = 10 kΩ, 1M = 1 MΩ.
Small trimmers use a 3-digit code: two digits, then the number of zeros. 103 = 10 followed by 3 zeros = 10 000 Ω = 10 kΩ.
example: B10K = linear, 10 kΩ. A trimmer marked 503 = 50 followed by 3 zeros = 50 kΩ.

tapers.name: Linear
tapers.meaning: The value changes evenly: half a turn gives half the resistance.
tapers.use: Arduino inputs, sensor thresholds, most projects

tapers.name: Logarithmic (audio)
tapers.meaning: Changes slowly at first, then quickly.
tapers.use: Volume controls, because our ears hear loudness on a log scale

tapers.name: Reverse logarithmic
tapers.meaning: Changes quickly at first, then slowly.

taperNote: Some older European pots used A for linear. If you are not sure, set the knob to the middle and measure with a multimeter: about half the value means linear.

types.name: Rotary potentiometer
types.looks: Round metal body with a shaft you turn about 300°, and three legs in a row.
types.note: Fit a knob cap on the shaft. The breadboard-friendly ones are usually 10 kΩ.

types.name: Slide potentiometer
types.looks: Long flat body with a lever that slides in a straight line.
types.note: Same idea as a rotary pot, just a straight track. Pins are often at both ends.

types.name: Trimmer (preset)
types.looks: Small blue square or round part turned with a small screwdriver.
types.note: Made to be set and left alone, not turned every day. Usually marked with a 3-digit code like 103.

types.name: Multi-turn trimmer (3296)
types.looks: Tall blue box with a brass screw on top that takes 10–25 turns from end to end.
types.note: Very precise. It may click at the ends; that is normal, it does not lock.

types.name: Dual-gang potentiometer
types.looks: Two rotary pots stacked on one shaft, with six legs.
uses: Changing two things with one knob
types.note: Both halves turn together, and each half has its own three pins.

types.name: Digital potentiometer
types.looks: A small chip (e.g. X9C103 or MCP4131) with no knob at all.
uses: Volume or gain set from code
types.note: The Arduino moves the wiper with signals (up/down pins or SPI). Keep voltages within the chip's supply.

values.purpose: Low value for fine control of small voltages.
uses: Variable LED current (with a fixed resistor in series)

uses: Knob on an analog pin with long wires

values.purpose: The standard Arduino potentiometer: perfect for analogRead().
Common for amplifier gain and comparator thresholds.
Draws less current, which suits battery projects.
The sensitivity trimmer found on many sensor modules.
uses: Sensitivity on IR and sound modules

values.purpose: High value for audio controls and timers.
Very high value for long timing and tiny currents.
